## UniPR-3D: Towards Universal Visual Place Recognition with Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer

Tianchen Deng 1 *, Xun Chen 3 *, Ziming Li 1 , Hongming Shen 3 , Danwei Wang 3 , Javier Civera 2 , Hesheng Wang 1 1 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2 I3A, University of Zaragoza, Spain 3 Nanyang Technological University

## Abstract

Visual Place Recognition (VPR) has been traditionally formulated as a single-image retrieval task. Using multiple views offers clear advantages, yet this setting remains relatively underexplored and existing methods often struggle to generalize across diverse environments. In this work we introduce UniPR-3D, the first VPR architecture that effectively integrates information from multiple views. UniPR3D builds on a VGGT backbone capable of encoding multiview 3D representations, which we adapt by designing feature aggregators and fine-tune for the place recognition task. To construct our descriptor, we jointly leverage the 3D tokens and intermediate 2D tokens produced by VGGT. Based on their distinct characteristics, we design dedicated aggregation modules for 2D and 3D features, allowing our descriptor to capture fine-grained texture cues while also reasoning across viewpoints. To further enhance generalization, we incorporate both single- and multi-frame aggregation schemes, along with a variablelength sequence retrieval strategy. Our experiments show that UniPR-3D sets a new state of the art, outperforming both single- and multi-view baselines and highlighting the effectiveness of geometry-grounded tokens for VPR. Our code and models will be made publicly available on Github https://github.com/dtc111111/UniPR-3D.

## 1. Introduction

Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is a core problem in robotics and computer vision, targeting the recognition of previously visited locations from visual observations [25, 38, 43, 45, 53, 69]. VPR plays a key role in fundamental tasks such as SLAM [15, 18, 42] and absolute pose estimation [50, 59, 71], which underpin a wide range of applications, including autonomous driving, robotic navigation, virtual and augmented reality.

VPR is typically formulated as a single-view retrieval task, in which a query image is used to retrieve an ordered

list of the topk matching candidates. Existing approaches generally rely on neural backbones to extract features, which are then aggregated using various strategies to form global image descriptors. Images are then represented by their aggregated appearance patterns, which are compared at test time via nearest-neighbor search. Backbone architectures have evolved from ResNet-based [3, 27, 49] to Vision Transformers (ViTs) [32, 62, 72]. Task-specific fine-tuned foundation models, in particular DINOv2 [48], achieve nowadays state-of-the-art performance [5, 29, 30]. Feature aggregation strategies have also advanced considerably, from the seminal NetVLAD [3], inspired by the handcrafted VLAD aggregation [31], to pooling-based methods such as GeM [49], MLP-based aggregations like MixVPR [2], and approaches leveraging optimal transport [30].

All these methods, however, share the fundamental limitation of extracting features from just one single view. Multiple views provide broader scene coverage and a richer variety of viewpoints, but multi-view feature aggregation has always been a challenging and relatively unexplored topic [21]. However, the recent development of the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) [61], a large ViT backbone able to model 3D spatial information from multiple views, has opened new possibilities for leveraging such information in various tasks. Building on this backbone for feature extraction, we introduce in this paper UniPR-3D, the first 3D token-based VPR framework supporting both single-frame and sequence-level place matching.

Our developments work as follows. For single-frame retrieval, we jointly utilize VGGT's 3D tokens and intermediate 2D tokens to construct the place descriptor. Based on the differences between token types, we design distinct aggregation strategies. For 2D tokens, we select the 2D CLS token, 2D register tokens, and 2D patch tokens for aggregation. For the 3D tokens, we discard the camera token (as VPR should be robust to viewpoint changes) and only use the 3D register tokens and 3D patch tokens to ensure stability under viewpoint changes. For patch tokens, we adopt an optimal transport approach [30] to derive local patch descriptors, while for register tokens, we employ GeM pooling [49] to generate their local descriptors.

For sequence-level retrieval, we define an anchor frame and multiple support frames, and construct a multi-frame feature aggregation method. We use SALAD in order to aggregate both 2D and 3D patch tokens across frames. For 3D register tokens as well as 2D CLS and register tokens, we design an aggregation that combines GeM pooling with an MLP-based projector. The token projector aligns the feature dimensions across different modalities and frames, enabling our network to process input sequences of arbitrary length. This design allows the model to generalize effectively to sequences with varying lengths during inference.

By incorporating 2D and 3D tokens, our system achieves universal place recognition capabilities across complex environments. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

By incorporating 2D and 3D tokens, our system achieves universal place recognition capabilities across complex environments. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

- We develop the first 3D token-based VPR method with tailored 2D and 3D feature aggregation methods, enabling universal generalization across diverse environments and supporting both single frame and sequence matching.
- We propose distinct aggregation strategies for different types of tokens. Specifically, register tokens are GeMpooled, as their number is relatively small, while patch tokens are aggregated using optimal transport to capture fine-grained spatial correspondences across frames.
- We introduce a sequence-level retrieval strategy, with an anchor frame and multiple support frames, and construct a multi-frame feature aggregation method, enabling our network to process input sequences of arbitrary length.

We evaluate UniPR-3D on a comprehensive and diverse set of public datasets under challenging conditions, in- cluding temporal variations, spatial changes, and viewpoint shifts. Our experimental results show that our method effectively leverages the information of multiple views and sets a new state of the art in such benchmarks.

## 2. Related work

VPR has made remarkable progress in recent years and has become a key component in tasks such as localization [17, 20, 37, 54], planning and control [35, 36, 39, 40, 65], autonomous driving [13, 64, 67, 68] and mixed reality [19]. Below, we review the most relevant advances in feature extraction, feature aggregation, and sequence-based retrieval. Feature Extraction. Early VPR methods relied on handcrafted visual descriptors, using either aggregated local features [31] or holistic global representations [47, 57]. Geometric and temporal consistency checks were often employed to improve robustness in practical systems [22, 46]. With the advent of deep learning, ResNet-based architectures became the standard for feature extraction [3]. More recently, Vision Transformer (ViT)-based foundation models [16] have shown superior representational power and generalization. For example, AnyLoc [32], SALAD [30], and UniLGL [55] leverage DINOv2 [48]: the former uses it directly, while the latter fine-tunes it for the VPR task. These models have demonstrated enhanced robustness to variations in illumination, weather, and viewpoint. Nevertheless, the vast majority of existing methods extract features from a single view, thus failing to exploit the spatial information available across multiple observations.

Feature Aggregation. The earliest aggregation schemes for VPR include Bag of Visual Words (BoW) [56] and Vector of Locally Aggregated Descriptors (VLAD) [31], both based on clustering handcrafted local descriptors. NetVLAD [3] extended VLAD by embedding it within a deep architecture that jointly learns the convolutional features and the aggregation process. The Generalized Mean Pooling (GeM) [49] of features, proposed later, was a widely used aggregation method combining simplicity and strong retrieval performance. MixVPR [2] introduced a MLP-based aggregation module to capture more expressive feature interactions. Recently, SALAD [30] proposed an aggregation based on optimal transport [9], achieving the current state of the art in feature aggregation for VPR.

Sequence Retrieval. To further boost the retrieval recall, a few methods have incorporated sequential inputs rather than individual frames. Most existing approaches [14, 46, 52] apply sequence-level similarity-based retrieval as a post-processing step over frame-level similarity scores. Learning-based methods [26, 44], instead, learn sequential descriptors to encode temporal dependencies or aggregate consecutive reference and query features into unified sequence-level representations [4, 23]. CaseVPR [34] further proposes a hierarchical sequence-to-frame retrieval pipeline combining coarse sequence retrieval with fine-grained frame alignment for accurate correspondence estimation. Despite these advances, existing sequence-based methods share two main limitations that hinder generalization. First, they rely on strong inductive biases, whereas our UniPR-3D, built upon VGGT and our learned aggregation modules, is more datadriven and thus more flexible. Second, these methods aggregate features purely along the temporal dimension, making them sensitive to changes in speed, frame rate, or sparsity of image sequences. In contrast, VGGT's features are geometrically grounded in 3D, enabling UniPR-3D to achieve greater robustness under such variations.

## 3. Method

We propose UniPR-3D, a universal visual place recognition framework that supports both frame-to-frame and sequenceto-sequence matching. The input to our method consists of an image sequence { I i } , and for sequence-level matching, we define an anchor frame and multiple support frames. Our model is capable of predicting visual descriptors for both individual frames and entire sequences. The framework is composed of three main modules: (i) Local 3D feature extraction (Sec. 3.1); (ii) Feature assignment and ag- gregation (Sec. 3.2). (iii) Sequence matching (Sec. 3.3). We elaborate on the entire pipeline of our system in the following subsections.

## 3.1. Local 3D Feature Extraction

Effective local feature extraction should remain robust under seasonal or day-to-night illumination changes, as well as viewpoint variations. This requires capturing sufficiently stable structural information. However, the most reliable cues for stability lie in the 3Dstructural information of the scene, whereas existing methods primarily focus on texturelevel feature extraction from a single image.

Existing methods such as AnyLoc [32] and SALAD [30] adopt DINOv2 [48] to extract local visual features, leveraging the exceptional representational capabilities of foundation models. However, these approaches do not capture spatial information. In UniPR-3D, we propose the first VPR framework based on the 3D tokens of a VGGT [61] backbone. Our framework follows a ViT-based architecture, in which every input image { I i } is first divided into patches p × p × c , which are sequentially processed through transformer blocks to generate different tokens.

Each image is first processed by the DINOv2 encoder to extract the 2D cls token , register token , and patch tokens , which primarily capture the texture-level characteristics of this image. Then we retain only the patch tokens as input to the subsequent alternating attention blocks and initialize

two additional tokens: a camera token , which encodes the camera intrinsics and extrinsics (including { R,T } , and the field-of-view parameters), and a register token . Through the alternating blocks composed of frame attention and global attention, the model produces three types of 3D tokens: a 3D camera token ( n × 1 ), 3D register tokens ( n × 4 ), and 3D patch tokens ( p × p ). To ensure viewpoint invariance of the final descriptor, we only preserve the 3D register and 3D patch tokens to capture both geometric and structural information of the environment, forming our 3D geometric descriptor.

## 3.3. Sequence Matching

For frame-to-frame matching, we directly take the image as input and obtain the corresponding 3D tokens. For sequence-to-sequence matching, we define an anchor frame and multiple support frames. In the VGGT architecture, the first frame is defined as the world coordinate system, with all tokens registered relative to anchor frame. This setup, along with the subsequent training pipeline, makes the first frame a crucial anchor for maintaining spatial consistency throughout the sequence. For multi-frame matching, we design a corresponding multi-frame feature aggregation strategy. Existing multi-frame fusion approaches typically support only fixed-length sequences, requiring the training and testing sequence lengths to be identical, which significantly limits generalization. To address this issue, we propose a variable-length sequence fusion framework. Specifically, we design a multi-frame projector based on Generalized Mean (GeM) pooling to aggregate the 2D CLS tokens, 2D register tokens, and 3D register tokens across frames, enabling flexible sequence-level feature fusion.

## 3.4. Training

For a fair comparison, we follow the experimental setups of two recent works: SALAD [30] for single-frame retrieval and SeqMatchNet [26] for sequence-level retrieval.

For single-frame training, we use GSV-Cities [1] as it is standard practice in the field. GSV-Cities is a large-scale collection of urban locations from Google Street View. For optimization, we adopt the multi-similarity loss [63] together with the AdamW optimizer [33]. For sequence-level training, since GSV-Cities does not support multi-frame training, we follow the setting of SeqMatchNet [26] and train our model on the Mapillary Street-Level Sequences (MSLS) dataset [66]. MSLS contains over 1.6 million images collected from the Mapillary collaborative mapping platform, covering diverse cities and exhibiting significant variations in viewpoint, weather, and illumination conditions. The training process consists of two stages: in the first stage, we train only the descriptor head; in the second stage, we jointly train the alternating attention blocks of VGGT and the DINOv2 encoder. All experiments are conducted using mixed-precision (FP16) training to improve computational efficiency and reduce memory consumption.

## 4. Experiments

To rigorously evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments following the standard evaluation protocols established in SALAD [30] for single-frame matching and follow SeqMatchNet [26] for sequence retrieval.

## 4.1. Implementation Details

Our model architecture follows VGGT [61] with L = 24 alternating frame and global attention layers. To accelerate inference, we incorporate FlashAttention-2 [12]. The model is initialized using pre-trained VGGT weights, and is trained for VPR using the AdamW optimizer with a hybrid learning rate schedule: a linear warm-up over the first 0.5 epochs, followed by cosine decay, with a peak learning rate of 1 × 10 -6 . All training are conducted on a NVIDIA A100 GPU. The inference speed is tested on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. For the 3D backbone, we adopt a LoRAbased fine-tuning strategy, where both the frame attention and global attention blocks are refined. For the cls descriptor and register descriptor, we employ dimensionality reduction, compressing the feature token dimensions to 256. In contrast, the patch descriptor is represented with a dimension of 128 × 64 = 8192 , with 64 clusters.

Dataset and Metrics For single-frame evaluation, We conduct experiments on a wide range of benchmark datasets to verify the generalization of our method. We use the validation and challenge partitions of MSLS [66], which consists of of dashcam images, Pittsburgh250k-test [60], imaging urban scenarios, NordLand [58] for its seasonal variations in train-front imagery across Norway, and SPED [10], recorded with surveillance cameras. We use Recall@k (R@k) as the evaluation metric for all experiments, following standard practice in the literature. We follow the evaluation protocol from SALAD [30] and MixVPR [2], where retrieval is considered correct if at least one image within 25 meters of the query location (or within two frames for the NordLand dataset) appears among the top-k candidates.

For multi-frame evaluation, we conduct experiments on the Nordland [58], MSLS [66], Oxford1 [41], and Oxford2 [41] datasets. Specifically, for Oxford1 we use 201412-16-18-44-24 (winter night) to 2014-1118-13-20-12 (fall day), sampled every 2 meters. And for Oxford2, 201411-14-16-34-33 (fall night) to 2015-11-13- 10-28-08 (fall day), sampled every 2 meters.

We adopt Recall@k (R@k) as the evaluation metric for all experiments. Differently from the single-frame setting, for the Oxford datasets, directly using a retrieval threshold of 25 meters often leads to saturated results (close to 100%) for existing methods. Therefore, we perform a more detailed evaluation using thresholds of 2 m and 25 m. For the Nordland dataset, retrieval is considered correct if the ground-truth frame within ten frames from the query appears among the topk retrieved candidates. Following CaseVPR [34], the sequence length S is set to be 5.

## 4.4. Conclusion

In this paper, we propose UniPR-3D, the first 3D tokenbased VPR method that supports universal scene recognition and outperforms previous baselines by a substantial margin. Moreover, our framework is capable of handling both frame-to-frame and sequence-level retrievals. We design 2D and 3D feature aggregation strategies tailored to the characteristics of different types of 2D and 3D tokens. For sequence-level retrieval, we further propose a multiframe feature aggregation method for variable-length sequence matching. The final descriptor is constructed by combining the 2D and 3D descriptors. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving strong performance in both single frame and sequence matching. This work provides new insights for the VPR community, highlighting the potential of transitioning from conventional 2D token-based descriptors to 3D token-based representations.

## A. Overview

In this supplementary material, we provide the implementation details and training details in Sec. B and Sec. C. In Sec. D, we conduct additional ablation studies. In Sec. F, we present extensive experimental results on various datasets.

## B. Implementation Details

Here we report the detailed settings and hyperparameters used in UniPR-3D to achieve universal visual place recognition. Our model architecture follows VGGT [61] with L = 24 alternating frame-attention and global-attention layers (12 layers each). To accelerate inference, we integrate FlashAttention-2 [12] to improve computational efficiency. For the cls descriptor and register descriptor, we apply dimensionality reduction and compress their token dimensions to 256. In contrast, each patch descriptor is represented with a dimension of 128 × 64 = 8192 using 64 clusters.

For the 2D and 3D patch tokens, we adopt a Conv-ReLU-Conv structure to produce the feature embeddings and corresponding assignment scores, which are then fed into the optimal transport module to obtain the final descriptor. For the 2D and 3D register tokens and the cls token, we use an MLP block followed by a GEM pooling layer and another MLP block; each MLP block consists of a linear layer, a ReLU activation, and a linear layer. All input images across datasets are uniformly cropped to a resolution of 392 × 518 , following the original VGGT preprocessing setup.

## C. Training Details

For the 3D backbone, we adopt a LoRA-based fine-tuning strategy in which both the frame-attention and globalattention blocks are refined. The model is initialized from the pre-trained VGGT weights and optimized using AdamW with a hybrid learning-rate schedule: a linear warm-up over the first 0.5 epochs followed by cosine decay, with a peak learning rate of 1 × 10 -6 . All training is conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, and inference speed is measured on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

We follow a two-stage training protocol. In Stage 1, we freeze the feature-extraction backbone and train only the feature aggregation and feature assignment networks-i.e., the parameters of the GEM pooling layers and the optimaltransport module. In Stage 2, we unfreeze the featureextraction blocks. Similar to SALAD [30], we observe that the weakly supervised contrastive objective becomes unstable when fully fine-tuning all global-attention blocks and Dino v2 blocks. Therefore, we only fine-tune the last few blocks, which yields better stability and overall per- formance. These findings are further validated through detailed ablation studies presented later in the paper.

## D. Ablation Study

In this section, we provide additional ablation studies evaluating the influence of retrieval distance.

Besides the main results reported in the paper, we further analyze the effect of retrieval distance on the Recall@k (R@k) evaluation metric. For single-frame matching, we follow the standard evaluation protocol used in SALAD [30] and MixVPR [2]: a retrieval is considered correct if at least one database image within 25 meters of the query location appears among the top-k candidates (or within two frames for the NordLand dataset).

For sequence matching, as described in the main paper, we additionally report results on the Oxford dataset under different retrieval distance thresholds (2 m and 25 m) to provide a more fine-grained comparison. In the supplementary material, we further extend this analysis by evaluating multiple datasets under a range of retrieval thresholds, as shown in Tab. 6.

For the NordLand dataset, our main results adopt the commonly used protocol that deems a retrieval correct if the retrieved frame is within ten frames of the query. To better understand robustness under stricter or looser matching criteria, we also experiment with alternative thresholds such as two frames and five frames, providing a comprehensive evaluation of retrieval sensitivity across distance settings. The results are shown in Tab. 6. We observe that our method achieves state-of-the-art results across all datasets under varying retrieval distance thresholds, fully demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. These results highlight the necessity and significance of introducing 3D tokens for visual place recognition, as they provide stable geometric cues that remain reliable under challenging viewpoint, illumination, and environmental changes.

In addition, we conclude experiments across different sequence lengths, as shown in Tab. 7. We observe that our method consistently maintains state-of-the-art performance as the sequence length varies. This demonstrates that, even when the test-time sequence length differs from that seen during training, our approach still exhibits strong generalization and achieves the best results across different datasets. These findings validate the effectiveness of our proposed multi-view feature aggregation strategy and highlight the importance of introducing multi-frame 3D tokens for sequence-level matching. Moreover, our method remains robust under challenging illumination changes, location shifts, and viewpoint variations, enabling reliable visual place recognition in diverse real-world conditions.

On the Nordland dataset, we follow standard practice and evaluate using frame-based thresholds at 1 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 , and 25 frames.
